title: Deferred schema fragmenter SDK patterns for streaming + tool calls
creator: Evelyn Park
description:
Goal: ship an SDK pattern that lets client libraries (TypeScript, Python, Go) consume high-throughput streaming responses that include interleaved typed tool/function calls and structured outputs while minimizing memory usage, enabling resumable sessions, and preserving strong typing via deferred/fragmented schema attachments.

Context: existing streaming adapters assume full-message JSON frames or protocol-level envelopes that vendors supply up-front. For large tool schemas (hundreds of fields) or evolving contracts we want clients to be able to: 1) accept compact fragment envelopes during low-latency stream emission, 2) lazily fetch full schema descriptions or tool manifests only when needed, and 3) reassemble typed objects in a deterministic, resumable way across language bindings.

Key behaviors and acceptance criteria:
- Server emits "fragmented envelopes": small stable header + fragment payload (base64 or raw) + fragment_id + optional schema_ref.
- Clients reconstruct typed objects by: (a) local cache lookup for schema_ref, (b) fallback to a lightweight schema fetch endpoint, (c) tolerant assembly when schema versions mismatch (apply convertors).
- Tool/function-calling remains first-class: tool invocation frames contain call_id, tool_name, argument_fragments (0..n). SDK exposes a single unified callback per invocation that yields partial argument updates as fragments arrive and a final assembled typed argument object once complete.
- Session resume: streams emit transcript_token and last_committed_fragment_id. Clients can reconnect and resume from last_committed_fragment_id to avoid re-executing side-effects. Resume flow must be safe for idempotent tool calls; non-idempotent tool calls must be flagged in the manifest.
- Cross-language API ergonomics (TS/Py/Go) must be idiomatic while preserving a shared wire contract and clear migration path from the existing framed JSON approach.

Design trade-offs discussed:
- Eager schema shipping vs deferred fetch: we favor deferred for latency and bandwidth on common paths, with a bounded TTL and prefetch heuristics for hot tools.
- Strong typing vs runtime resilience: SDKs should provide typed wrappers but expose an "unstructured" fallback for partial assembly or unknown fields to avoid hard failures.
- Memory vs CPU: fragmented assembly reduces peak memory but increases CPU for reassembly; benchmarks below guide defaults.

Implementation plan (milestones):
1) Design doc + wire contract (this ticket) — finalize envelope fields, resume semantics, schema endpoint shape.
2) Server prototype (runtime team) emits fragmented envelopes behind a feature flag.
3) TypeScript SDK prototype: ergonomics-first, with example helpers for React/Next streaming.
4) Python SDK prototype: generator-based streaming that yields Fragment events and final Assembled objects.
5) Go SDK prototype: channel-based assembler optimized for low-allocation paths.
6) Cross-language examples, docs, and migration guide.
7) Canary rollout and perf/compat tests; migrate docs and announce.

API summary examples (high-level signatures):
TypeScript (consumer pattern):
- onFragment(cb: (f: FragmentEnvelope) => void): Subscription
- assembleToolCall(sessionId, callId): Promise<TypedToolArgs> // resolves when fragments complete or throws when unrecoverable
- resumeStream(transcriptToken, fromFragmentId) => AsyncIterable<StreamEvent>

Python (consumer pattern):
- async for ev in client.stream(...):
- 	if ev.type == 'fragment': handle_fragment(ev)
- 	if ev.type == 'tool_result' and ev.call_complete: result = await client.assemble_tool_call(ev.call_id)

Go (consumer pattern):
- events := client.Stream(ctx, req)
- for ev := range events { switch ev.Kind { case Fragment: assembler.Add(ev) ... } }
- args, err := assembler.WaitFor(callID)

Detailed migration and compatibility notes:
- SDK will ship a compatibility shim that accepts the old framed JSON payloads and routes them through the same assembler API, so existing consumers can opt-in with minimal changes.
- For third-party tool manifests, we attach a "compat_hint" that maps legacy field names to canonical names during assembly.

Performance and safety guardrails (benchmarks):
- Target: <= 3% median latency increase for typical short-chat streams; memory peak reduced by ~40% for heavy tool payloads (>1MB tool argument aggregates) in the deferred-flow.
- Safety: server will mark non-idempotent tool calls with a header; SDK defaults to not auto-retry these on resume.

Testing and rollout plan:
- Unit: fragment assembly edge cases (missing fragments, out-of-order, duplicate).
- Integration: cross-lang roundtrip tests using synthetic tool manifests at scale.
- Canary: enable feature flag for 5% of hosted traffic with runtime-level observability counters for fragment loss, reassembly failures, and resume success rates.

Acceptance criteria (concrete):
- TypeScript / Python / Go SDK prototypes exist with example apps and documented signatures.
- Cross-lang example shows tool call with 7 fragments reassembled deterministically and resume after a simulated disconnect.
- Perf regression <5% in P50 latency for typical streams.
- Migration doc and an automated codemod recipe for TS clients to switch to assembler API.

Deliverables:
- design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/Deferred+Fragment+Wire+Contract (link)
- prototype PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1159 , https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-ts/pull/243 , https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-py/pull/87 , https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-go/pull/52
- example apps: SDK-examples/stream-fragmenter (internal drive)

2026-03-09 - QA (Marco Silva): Added test cases for duplicate fragment and missing fragment recovery. Found edge case where converters drop unknown enum values—added acceptance criterion to preserve unknown enums in unstructured fallback.

notes: Follow-up: add a small TypeScript migration codemod to convert old stream handlers to assembler pattern.
Consider an optional bundle with precompiled converters for common tool manifests to reduce assembly CPU cost.
Document failure modes clearly: missing fragments, schema not found, incompatible version -> fall back to unstructured payloads and surface telemetry.
Plan A/B test for eager schema shipping vs deferred in a single region to measure actual bandwidth savings and latency trade-offs.
